text: Retrieval metrics For one query q, the labels give a set of relevant passages Rel(q), each with a grade (binary: relevant or not; graded: for example 3 = answers the question on its own, 2 = holds a needed part, 1 = related background, 0 = irrelevant).
label: owned:models_and_training/topic_ml_fundamentals/evaluation_metrics

text: The retriever returns a ranked list, and a metric "at k" looks only at the top k, because only those reach the prompt.
label: owned:models_and_training/topic_ml_fundamentals/evaluation_metrics
key: precision@k is the share of the top k

text: Each metric is computed per query and averaged over the queries; TREC's trec_eval and its Python binding pytrec_eval are the reference implementations, and BEIR and MTEB use them. recall@k = |Rel(q) ∩ Top k (q)| / |Rel(q)| precision@k = |Rel(q) ∩ Top k (q)| / k hit@k = 1 if any relevant passage is in Top k (q), else 0 RR = 1 / rank of the first relevant passage DCG@k = Σ i=1..k gain(rel i ) / log 2 (i+1) nDCG@k = DCG@k / IDCG@k Top k (q) the first k retrieved passages rel i the grade of the passage at rank i (0 if unjudged or irrelevant) gain linear, gain = rel (what trec_eval , BEIR and MTEB use), or exponential, gain = 2 rel − 1 (Burges et al.
label: core

text: 2005, used by some learning-to-rank libraries); the two give different numbers on graded labels IDCG@k the DCG of the ideal order, all relevant passages sorted by grade, so nDCG lies in [0, 1] MRR the mean of RR over queries, often cut at 10 (RR = 0 when the first hit is below rank 10) recall@k is the number RAG lives on: if the evidence is not in the prompt nothing downstream can recover it.
label: owned:models_and_training/topic_ml_fundamentals/evaluation_metrics

text: Measure it twice, at the k that reaches the prompt and at the depth the reranker reads (often 50 to 150), or a retrieval miss and a ranking miss look the same.
label: core

text: It has no value for a query with no relevant passage (an unanswerable question): leave those out of the average and score abstention on them instead. hit@k (also "success@k", or "recall@k" in some dense-retrieval papers, which use the name for this per-query 0 or 1) equals recall@k when every query has exactly one relevant passage, and is more lenient otherwise.
label: core
key: recall@k has no value for an unanswerable question

text: Check which one a paper means before comparing. precision@k penalises padding the prompt: raising k can only raise recall and usually lowers precision.
label: core

text: It is capped by the labels: with one relevant passage per query, precision@10 cannot exceed 0.1.
label: core

text: MRR fits single-answer lookups and ignores everything after the first hit. nDCG@10 rewards putting the most relevant passage first; it is the standard for comparing rerankers, whose whole job is moving items up, and BEIR's and MTEB's headline retrieval number.
label: core

text: A real run, scored and reproduced To see what the metrics say on real labels, we ran five retrievers over three BEIR test sets ( Thakur et al., NeurIPS 2021 Datasets and Benchmarks ) and scored them against the released qrels: SciFact (5,183 abstracts, 300 scientific claims), NFCorpus (3,633 medical documents, 323 queries, graded labels 1 and 2) and FiQA-2018 (57,638 financial forum posts, 648 questions).

label: core
key: a faithfulness metric is an llm judge with a fixed prompt

text: Faithfulness (groundedness) Split the answer into atomic claims and ask, claim by claim, whether the retrieved passages support it: faithfulness = claims in the answer supported by the passages / claims in the answer RAGAS's own example: the passage says Einstein was born on 14 March 1879 in Germany; the answer says "Einstein was born in Germany on 20th March 1879".
label: core
key: faithfulness = claims in the answer supported by the passages / claims in the answer

text: The judge splits it into "born in Germany" (supported) and "born on 20th March 1879" (not supported), so faithfulness = 1/2 = 0.5 ( RAGAS docs ).
label: core

text: Low faithfulness is hallucination despite retrieval.
label: fat

text: Two things it is not: Not correctness.
label: core

text: It checks the answer against the passages, not the passages against the world.
label: core
key: faithfulness and citation accuracy compare the answer with the passages only

label: core

text: Freshness and source checks are a separate test.
label: core
key: freshness and source checks are a separate test

text: Not the same as "true".
label: core

text: RAGTruth's annotators flagged whether each hallucinated span was nevertheless true in the world ( implicit_true ): 846 of the 2,927 question-answering spans were (28.9%; the model filled the gap from memory, correctly).
label: core

text: A faithfulness metric counts them as failures, which is right for a system that must answer from its sources and wrong if you only care about accuracy.

text: Answer relevance Does the answer address the question?
label: core
key: does the answer address the question?

text: It says nothing about truth: Llama-2-13B's answer in the animation is about whether Kenneth Williams is alive, true, and irrelevant.
label: core

text: RAGAS measures it backwards: an LLM writes N questions the answer would answer (N = 3 by default), and the score is their mean cosine similarity to the real question in embedding space.
label: core

text: In RAGAS's code, not its docs, the score is set to 0 when the judge flags every generated question as noncommittal ("I don't know"; _answer_relevance.py , February 2026).
label: core

text: DeepEval measures it forwards, as the share of the answer's statements that are relevant to the question.
label: core

text: Same name, different instruments: the next section sets them side by side.
label: fat

text: Context relevance and context precision Graded on the retrieved passages, but by a judge rather than by labels, so they work without qrels.
label: core
key: relevance judged per passage against the reference answer

text: Context relevance (TruLens) asks whether each retrieved passage is relevant to the question.
label: core
key: trulens's context relevance asks only whether each passage is relevant

text: Context precision (RAGAS) asks whether the relevant passages were ranked above the irrelevant ones: context precision@K = Σ k=1..K (precision@k × v k ) / (relevant passages in the top K) v k the judge's 0 or 1 verdict on the passage at rank k (against the reference answer, or against the response when there is none) It is the average precision of the judged list.
label: core
key: the average precision of the judged list

text: Irrelevant passages ranked above relevant ones lower it; irrelevant passages ranked below every relevant one do not, so one relevant passage at rank 1 followed by nine misses scores 1.0 while precision@10 is 0.1 (the third preset in the calculator above).
label: core
key: padding the prompt is invisible to context precision

text: On the worked example with binary verdicts, the first-stage list (relevant at ranks 2 and 4) scores (1/2 + 2/4) / 2 = 0.5 and the reranked list (ranks 1, 2 and 4) scores (1 + 1 + 3/4) / 3 = 0.917.
label: core

text: Context recall The share of the reference answer's claims that the retrieved passages could support: the judged cousin of retrieval recall, usable when you have reference answers but no passage labels.
label: core
key: the judged cousin of retrieval recall

text: A reference answer with 4 claims of which the passages support 3 scores 0.75: a quarter of what a correct answer needs never reached the generator.
label: core
key: 4 claims of which the passages support 3 scores 0.75

text: Citation accuracy When the system cites, check the citations themselves.
label: core

text: ALCE ( Gao et al., EMNLP 2023 ) splits the answer into statements, each citing a set of passages C i , and uses an NLI model (TRUE, a T5-11B fine-tuned for entailment) as the checker: citation recall of a statement is 1 if it cites at least one passage and the cited passages, concatenated, entail it; averaged over statements; citation precision of a citation is 0 if it is "irrelevant": it does not entail the statement on its own, and the other citations entail the statement without it; averaged over citations.
label: core
key: true, a t5-11b fine-tuned for entailment

text: Redundant but supporting citations are not penalised.
label: core
key: redundant but supporting citations are not penalised

text: ALCE's headline: on ELI5, even the best models of 2023 lacked complete citation support about half the time.
label: core

text: Citation checks are the cheapest groundedness test in production, because they need no reference answer and the NLI check is a small model; their blind spot is a claim left uncited.

section: judging faithfulness with an llm, and how it fails
text: Judging faithfulness with an LLM, and how it fails A faithfulness metric is an LLM judge with a fixed prompt, so it inherits the judge's position, verbosity and self-preference biases and its drift across versions; LLM-as-judge owns the catalogue and the calibration method (a few hundred hand-labelled items, Cohen's kappa, the pass rate corrected for the judge's measured error rates).
